name: Eintal
description: Eintal (The Enchanter) is a supernatural being in Norwegian folklore associated with lakes and bodies of water, particularly in the Telemark region of Eastern Norway (Østlandet). The eintal is related to the nøkken but is specifically a water-dwelling spirit that enchants people with music. The name comes from ein meaning one/lone and tal meaning speech/song, suggesting a solitary singer. Eintal legends tell of a beautiful but dangerous being who sits by lakes playing a harp or Hardanger fiddle, enchanting listeners into the water. Unlike the nøkken who drowns victims, the eintal is more subtle - the listener is simply compelled to enter the water, drawn by the overwhelming beauty of the music. The eintal represents the specifically Telemark version of the dangerous water spirit, distinct from the nøkken of other regions. The Hardanger fiddle, Norway's national instrument, is central to eintal stories
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: El Coco
description: El Coco (also known as El Cuco) is the bogeyman figure of the Spanish-speaking world, a ghost-like monster used for centuries to frighten children into good behavior. Originating in 17th-century Iberia and brought to the Americas through Spanish colonization, El Coco is described as a shapeless, shadowy figure with glowing red eyes that hides in closets, under beds, or in dark corners. The classic Spanish lullaby warns: 'Duérmete niño, duérmete ya... Que viene el Coco y te comerá' (Sleep child, sleep now... Or the Coco will come and eat you). In the Mexican-American communities of the US Southwest, El Coco is sometimes called the 'Coco Man' and is described as a hunchbacked figure who carries a sack to collect misbehaving children. Some versions depict him as a hairy monster, while others as a shapeshifter who takes the form of any dark shadow. Unlike many Hispanic folklore figures that have narrative stories, El Coco is primarily a disciplinary tool invoked through lullabies and warnings rather than tales
source: Latino folklore — El Coco bogeyman documented across Latin American oral tradition.

name: El Cucuy
description: El Cucuy is a distinct Mexican and Mexican-American variant of the bogeyman legend, particularly prevalent among Chicano families in the US Southwest. Unlike the more generic El Coco, El Cucuy is specifically described as a small, hairy, goblin-like creature who lives under children's beds or in dark closets, waiting to grab ankles or drag away children who refuse to sleep. Some accounts describe him with red or yellow eyes, long claws, and a mischievous grin. The legend serves dual purposes: as a parenting tool to enforce bedtime and as a cultural rite of passage where children learn to face their fears. In recent decades, El Cucuy has been reimagined in Chicano literature and art as a symbol of the fears faced by immigrant children — the unknown terrors of a new country, border crossing, and cultural displacement. Writers like Rudolfo Anaya have explored the Cucuy as a metaphor for the shadow side of the American Dream. Unlike the Iberian El Coco which is more formless, El Cucuy has a distinctly goblin-like personality and physical form
source: Mexican-American folklore — El Cucuy bogeyman documented in Hispanic oral tradition.

name: El Duende
description: A SMALL, GNOMELIKE CREATURE from Spanish and Latin American folklore with a prominent place in Mexican-American oral tradition of the US Southwest. Described as a tiny old man or child-like figure wearing a large hat and carrying a walking stick, El Duende lives in forests, caves, abandoned buildings, and rural areas. His most distinctive feature is his backward feet, making it easy to identify his tracks but difficult to follow him. He is known for playing tricks on humans — stealing food, hiding objects, tangling hair, leading travelers in circles through the woods, and making strange noises at night. In more dangerous versions, El Duende tries to capture children who wander away from their parents, keeping them as his own. In the curanderismo tradition, encounters with duendes are believed to cause illness, particularly susto (fright sickness), which requires a limpieza (spiritual cleansing) performed by a curandero. Among Hispanic families in the Southwest, stories of El Duende serve to keep children close to home and explain the mysterious sounds and occurrences of rural life. The duende can be helpful if treated with respect — offering food or tobacco may earn his favor
source: Latin American folklore; la duende is a mischievous dwarf spirit common in various regions.

name: El Jinete Sin Cabeza
description: El Jinete Sin Cabeza (The Headless Horseman) is a Hispanic variant of the headless horseman legend from the Rio Grande Valley and northern Mexico. Unlike the more famous Ichabod Crane version, this specter is specifically rooted in the borderlands' history of conflict. He is said to be the ghost of a Spanish conquistador or Mexican rancher who lost his head in battle — either during the Mexican War of Independence or the Mexican-American War. He rides a black horse through the moonlit mesquite at midnight, carrying his severed head under his arm. His appearance is a fearsome omen: to see him foretells death, war, or disaster. If you encounter him, you must not look into the eyes of his severed head, or you will be doomed to ride beside him forever. Some Chicano versions connect the legend to specific historical events like the Battle of the Alamo or the signing of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, making the supernatural figure a symbol of Mexican dispossession and the violent history of the border
source: Mexican-American/Southwestern folklore — the Headless Horseman documented in Hispanic and Anglo-American oral tradition.

name: Nahual
description: El Nahual (or Nagual) is a shapeshifting witch or sorcerer from Mesoamerican tradition with deep roots in Aztec and Maya cosmology. The belief, originating with the Nahua peoples, holds that certain individuals possess the spiritual power to transform into animals — most commonly jaguars, coyotes, dogs, owls, or turkeys. In Aztec tradition, each person is born with a tonal (animal spirit companion) linked to their birth date, but only those with special power (nagualism) can actually assume the animal's form. The god Tezcatlipoca was the protector of nagualism. During the colonial period, Indigenous shamans were conflated with European witchcraft beliefs. In Mexican-American folklore of the Southwest, nahuales are feared for their ability to cause illness, steal livestock, and harm enemies. In some Indigenous communities, however, the nahual is a respected protector of the people and natural resources. The nagual was popularized in English by Carlos Castaneda's controversial books, but authentic nagualism remains a living tradition in rural Mexico and among Mexican-American communities
source: Mesoamerican folklore; the Nahual is a shapeshifting sorcerer who transforms into animals.

name: El Silbón
description: El Silbón (The Whistler) is a terrifying specter from the folklore of Mexico's northern plains and the US Southwest borderlands. He is described as a tall, thin figure dressed in white, carrying a bundle of bones on his back — the remains of his murdered father. His most distinctive feature is his whistle: a melody that begins softly and grows increasingly louder, signaling his approach. The whistle has a unique property — if it sounds close, the Silbón is far away; snip if it sounds distant, he is right behind you. According to legend, the Silbón was a young man who murdered his father after the father killed the young man's wife. As punishment, the grandfather cursed him to wander forever carrying his father's bones, pursued by rabid demon dogs. He is said to suck the alcohol out of drunkards through their navel, tear womanizers to pieces, and add their bones to his sack. The only things that can save a victim are the sound of a barking dog, chili peppers, or a whip. In Mexican-American communities, El Silbón is a warning against family violence, drunkenness, and nighttime wandering
source: Venezuelan llanos folklore — El Silbón whistling spirit documented in Venezuelan oral tradition.

source: Mexican/Venezuelan folklore — El Silbón whistling spirit documented in oral tradition.

name: El Sombrerón
description: El Sombrerón (The Big-Hatted One) is a legendary goblin-like figure from Guatemalan and southern Mexican folklore who is particularly prominent in Mexican-American storytelling. He is described as a small man — no taller than a child — wearing an enormous hat, a red tie, and riding a tiny horse or mule. El Sombrerón is best known for braiding the manes and tails of horses, donkeys, and mules into intricate patterns that cannot be undone. He also bothers young women with long hair and big eyes by serenading them under their windows with a tiny silver guitar, causing them to fall into a deep melancholy or sleeplessness. He puts soil in their food so they cannot eat. His enchantment can only be broken by cutting the victim's hair and having a priest bless it with holy water. In some versions, El Sombrerón stuffs his victims with food and sugar until they die of sweetness. The legend advises teenage girls to preserve traditional values and warns against vanity and nighttime wandering
source: Guatemalan folklore — El Sombrerón is a goblin figure documented in Guatemalan oral tradition.

name: Elegua
description: Yoruba Orisha (deity) of roads, crossroads, and messenger of the gods. Known as Èṣù-Ẹlẹ́gbára (also Eleggua, Eshu, Legba). First AND Last to be invoked - all ceremonies in Santería must receive Elegua's approval before progressing. THE Gatekeeper who holds keys to past, present, and future. Opens and closes paths of destiny, controls opportunity and choice. Also a Trickster - creates chaos or favorable outcomes, embodies opposites. Can appear as Child (mischievous, playful) or OLD MAN (wise), representing different phases of fate and life. Colors: RED, Black, White. Numbers: 3 and 21. Associated with Ogun (war), Oshun (love/river), Yemoja (mother of waters). In Cuba's Santería, Brazil's Candomblé, Haiti's Vodou - remains central. Translated via slave trade. Symbolizes choice at crossroads - every decision passes through Elegua's domain
source: Nigeria mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Eloko
description: Eloko is a spirit from Central African Republic mythology. These forest-dwelling creatures are believed to be the restless spirits of ancestors who died with unresolved grudges, condemned to haunt the darkest, densest parts of the rainforest. Unlike benevolent spirits, the Eloko are fiercely territorial and vengeful, guarding their forest treasures including game animals and rare plants. They are known to cast spells on trespassers using enchanted bells that paralyze their victims before they attack. The Eloko embody the Mongo-Nkundo belief that the dead can return to settle scores with the living, serving as both a warning to honor one's ancestors and a caution against exploiting forest resources without proper respect. They share similarities with other Central African forest spirits such as the Sasabonsam of Ghana
source: https://www.mythologicalcreatures.net/categories/culture/african/central-african / https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eloko

name: Eloko
description: The Eloko (singular: Eloko or Eloki) are dwarf-like, vicious ancestral spirits from the mythology of the Mongo-Nkundo people of the Democratic Republic of Congo. These forest-dwelling creatures are believed to be the restless spirits of ancestors who died with unresolved grudges, condemned to haunt the darkest, densest parts of the rainforest. Unlike benevolent spirits, the Eloko are fiercely territorial and vengeful, guarding their forest treasures including game animals and rare plants. They are known to cast spells on trespassers using enchanted bells that paralyze their victims before they attack. The Eloko embody the Mongo-Nkundo belief that the dead can return to settle scores with the living, serving as both a warning to honor one's ancestors and a caution against exploiting forest resources without proper respect. They share similarities with other Central African forest spirits such as the Sasabonsam of Ghana
source: Congolese folklore — forest spirit documented in DR Congo oral tradition.

source: Mongo-Nkundo oral tradition

name: Enkai (Engai)
description: Enkai, also known as Engai, is the supreme god of the Maasai people of Kenya and Tanzania. Enkai is neither male nor female but manifests in two distinct aspects: Enkai Narok (the Black God), who is benevolent and brings rain, grass, and prosperity, and Enkai Na-nyokie (the Red God), who is vengeful and brings drought, lightning, and famine. According to Maasai cosmology, Enkai once lived on earth with humanity but withdrew into the sky after being displeased. Before leaving, Enkai lowered cattle from heaven on a leather thong through a sacred fig tree, entrusting them to the Maasai as their sacred guardians. Enkai's dual nature reflects the balance of the Maasai world -- the life-giving rains and destructive droughts. Prayers to Enkai are offered at the sacred mountain Oldoinyo Lengai (Mountain of God) and beneath wild fig trees (oreteti). Enkai is associated with black (good disposition) and red (anger), visible in the clouds
source: Maasai oral tradition, Encyclopedia of African Religion, Google Arts and Culture - Project FUEL

name: Eototo
description: Hopi Kachina (Katsina) - Chief OF ALL Kachinas and spiritual counterpart to the village chief. Called the 'father' of all kachinas, knows ALL ceremonies. Controls seasons and weather - especially Rain, the most-critical element for Hopi agriculture in the arid Southwest. Appears at Powamu Ceremony (February bean planting festival) and other key rituals. Derived From: Ometeotl (Aztec creator god) - 'goes to the north end of the kiva' ritual connects to 'Red Land of the south' journey. With Aholi (second-in-command, handsome), traveled to the Red Land and brought back squash/gifts of nature. Husband of Hahai-i Wuhti. Unlike Aholi, Eototo has Shabby, dull appearance but powers should NOT be judged by looks. At Powamu, draws cornmeal cloud symbols on ground, pours sacred water from his gourd into hatchway for blessing. Controls every gust of wind. Represents essential life force governing ceremonial cycles
source: Hopi spiritual tradition; documented in Southwestern ethnographic records.

name: Erik Munks Gjenferd
description: Erik Munks gjenferd is the ghost of Erik Munk (1530s-1590s), a ruthless 16th-century mine owner who operated the Barbu silver and copper mines near Arendal. According to legend, Munk acquired land through fraud — he tricked a man named Benkestok into swearing an oath on what the man thought was his own land, while Munk had secretly placed soil from that land in the man's shoes. After his death, Munk was condemned to become a deildegast (boundary ghost), endlessly wandering the boundaries of his ill-gotten lands. However, unlike the typical deildegast who carries a boundary stone, Erik Munk's ghost haunts specifically the mining district of Barbu outside Arendal. His ghost is said to appear at the old mine entrances and along the paths between Arendal and Barbu. He represents the shadow side of Arendal's mining prosperity, reflecting the harsh conditions and exploitative practices of early Norwegian mining
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Erlkönig
description: The Erlkönig (Erl-King) is a sinister figure from German and Danish folklore, most famously immortalized in Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's 1782 ballad Erlkönig and later set to music by Franz Schubert. The name is a mistranslation of the Danish ellerkonge (elf-king), which German translators confused with Erle (alder tree), literally creating king of the alders. In the ballad, the Erlkönig is a supernatural entity who appears to a dying child, offering him beautiful games, flowers, and the company of his daughters. The father, riding desperately through the night with his sick son in his arms, cannot see the Erlkönig but hears his voice coaxing the child toward death. In Danish tradition, the ellerkonge is the king of the ellefolk (elves), who lives in an elf-hill and presides over the nightly dances of the hidden people
source: German folklore; the Erlkönig is the king of the elves in German tradition.

name: Erlking
description: Malevolent ELF-King from Germanic folklore. Name: German 'Erlkönig' = 'Alder-King' (NOT 'elf' - mistranslation from Danish 'elverkonge' = 'elf-king'). Origin: Johann Gottfried Herder adapted Danish folk ballad 'Elveskud' (Elves' Shot) into German as 'Erlkönigs Tochter' (Erl-King's Daughter). Goethe then created his famous 1782 ballad where the antagonist IS the Erlking himself (changed from original daughter). Danish Original: elverkongens datter (elf-king's daughter) - female spirit who tempts nobleman, strikes him when refused. Goethe'S Version: Father rides with feverish son at night. Child sees Erlking and his 'daughters' (golden robes, dancing, games). Father sees only mist/willow trees. Erlking threatens 'Gewalt' (force) if boy won't come willingly. Boy dies - father finds him dead on arrival. IN Scandinavia: ellekonge - king of the elves, lives in forests, stalks children. Touch Kills immediately. Lures with promises of joy, golden clothes, his daughters' companionship. Connected to 'Alveskud' ballad (woman rejects elf-lover, elf shoots her)
source: German folklore; the Erlking is a malevolent forest spirit in German tradition.

name: Eshu
description: Yoruba Orisha (deity) of Trickery, Crossroads, Duality, and Languages. Differs From Elegua but Closely Related - some say they are brothers, some same being (256 paths for Elegua vs 101 for Eshu in Santería). Primary Trickster - causes mischief to teach lessons, plays jokes, creates chaos. Messenger between Ajogun (malevolent spirits), Orishas (benevolent), and humans. Speaks ALL languages. Dual Nature: both good and evil, right and wrong, cleverness and vanity, violence and lust. In Cuba: 'Eleguá moves silently, Echu breaks through forcefully.' In Palo Mayombe (Colombia): 'Exu.' In Haitian Vodou: 'Papa Legba' - wise old man with cane, opens gate between worlds. In Candomblé: 'Exu de Candomblé.' Creator of mischief and teacher - his trickery exposes human folly. Carries sacrifices to Orishas. In Ifá divination: 256 paths to Elegua are all Eshu manifestations. Participated in world creation alongside Obatalá, Olorum, Odudua. 'Eshu Bi' = stern/forceful avatar - old man AND young boy. 'Eshu Ayé' works with all Orishas including Olokun, walks beach shores. 'Father who gave birth to Ogboni' (secret society)
source: Nigeria mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Mvelincanti
aliases: He Who Was There from the Beginning
description: Mvelincanti (meaning 'He Who Was There from the Beginning') is the supreme creator god in traditional Swazi religion of Eswatini. Unlike the more actively involved deities in some African pantheons, Mvelincanti is considered too remote and transcendent to be directly involved in the daily affairs of humanity. Instead, the Swazi people direct their worship and petitions primarily toward the ancestral spirits known as emadloti, who act as intermediaries between the supreme creator and the living. This theological structure reflects a common pattern in Southern Bantu religions where the high god is acknowledged as the ultimate source of all existence but is too distant for everyday worship. Mvelincanti is credited with creating the world, humanity, and the natural order, after which he withdrew from direct engagement with creation. The Swazi monarchy, particularly the king, traditionally held a semi-divine status as an intermediary between Mvelincanti, the ancestors, and the people, reinforcing the sacred nature of Swazi kingship
source: Wikipedia - Religion in Eswatini; Mythlok - Swazi Mythology; MexicoHistorico - Legends of Eswatini

name: Tikoloshe
description: The Tikoloshe (also spelled Tokoloshe or Thokolosi) is a malevolent dwarf-like water spirit found in the folklore of the Nguni peoples of Southern Africa, including the Swazi of Eswatini, Zulu, and Xhosa. This mischievous and often dangerous creature is typically described as a small, hairy humanoid standing between half a meter to one meter tall, with grotesque features including a large head, sharp teeth, clawed fingers, and glowing eyes. According to tradition, Tikoloshe are not naturally occurring spirits but are created by witch doctors (sangomas) to harm enemies or serve their masters. They can become invisible by swallowing a pebble, allowing them to move undetected. Tikoloshe are nocturnal beings that hide under beds, cause illness, steal vitality, and create domestic chaos. Children are warned to behave lest the Tikoloshe get them. The creature reflects traditional Southern African beliefs about witchcraft, spiritual danger, and the importance of maintaining proper spiritual protection through traditional healers
source: Old Folklore - Tokoloshe; GodsAndMonsters - Tikoloshe; MythBeasts - Tikoloshe; ColdMystery

name: Etügen
description: Etügen Eke ("Mother Earth") is the supreme earth goddess in Mongolian and Turkic Tengrist mythology. She is the second highest deity after Kök-Tengri (the Eternal Blue Sky) and is considered perpetually virginal. Etügen governs all natural forces and all living beings are subordinate to her. She is the patroness of homeland, nature, fertility, and the cycle of seasons. The name Etügen may derive from Ötüken, the sacred mountain of the ancient Turks. Medieval sources sometimes confused her with a male counterpart named Natigai, but this is believed to be a mispronunciation. Etügen existed in the middle of the universe and together with Tengri she maintains cosmic balance. Sacrifices were made to appease her every spring before cattle-breeding and planting, and every autumn after the harvest. A reddish horse was typically sacrificed near rivers and lakes to appeal for fertility and well-being
source: Mongolian folk religion — Etgen spirits.

name: Evil One (Cheyenne)
description: In Cheyenne tradition, the Evil One represents the malevolent forces that threaten the harmony of the community and the natural world. Cheyenne cosmology recognizes various evil or harmful spirits that can cause sickness, misfortune, and death. The most feared of these is the Two-Face (Hestovatohkeo'o), a monster with a second face on the back of its head that kills anyone who makes eye contact with it. Other malevolent beings include the Rolling Head, a disembodied vampiric head that seeks revenge for betrayal; the Ma'xemestaa'e, a hairy humanoid with birdlike feet; and various water monsters (Mehne or Axxea) that lurk in springs and menace travelers. The Cheyenne believe that humans who commit grave wrongs or die unnaturally may also return as wandering evil spirits, traveling the Short Fork of the Milky Way (the "suicide road") and returning to plague the living
source: Cheyenne spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous ethnographic records.

name: Fakse
description: Fakse is a type of carved wooden cult idol from the Setesdal region of Sørlandet, representing a rare survival of pre-Christian worship practices into the 19th century. The most famous fakse figures were Fakse-Brokke (from Brokke farm in Valle) and another from Rygnestad — male wooden figures about one meter tall, carved from pine. Farmers offered beer, butter, and food to the fakse, believing it would bring prosperity, protect livestock, and ensure good harvests. If the fakse was moved or disrespected, it would cause cattle disease and misfortune. The fakse tradition persisted in Setesdal until the mid-1800s when Christian authorities destroyed or removed the figures. The fakse represents the survival of Norse cult practices (similar to the worship of the Norse gods through idols) in the isolated mountain valley of Setesdal, where Christianity arrived later and blended with older traditions
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Famadihana
description: The Famadihana is not a creature but the honored ancestor spirit at the center of the Malagasy "turning of the bones" ceremony, a funerary tradition practiced primarily by the Merina and Betsileo peoples of Madagascar's central highlands. Known as razana (ancestors), these spirits remain intimately involved in the daily lives of their descendants long after death. The famadihana ceremony occurs roughly every five to seven years, when families exhume the bodies of their ancestors from family crypts, rewrap them in fresh silk shrouds (lambamena), and dance with the corpses while carrying them over their heads. The ceremony reaffirms the bond between the living and the dead. The razana are believed to become cold and uncomfortable in their old wrappings, and the famadihana warms them both literally and symbolically while rewriting their names on the new shrouds so they will never be forgotten
source: Malagasy funerary tradition — the "turning of the bones" ceremony documented in Malagasy culture.

name: Fanahy
description: The fanahy is a core concept in Malagasy spirituality, referring to the spirit or essence that determines an individual's character, behavior, and moral nature. Unlike the European concept of a singular soul, Malagasy tradition recognizes multiple spiritual components within a person, with fanahy being the moral and spiritual force that shapes personality. A person can have a "good fanahy" (generous, kind, socially harmonious) or a "bad fanahy" (stingy, angry, antisocial). When a person dies, the fanahy departs permanently from the body. If the deceased receives proper burial rites and famadihana ceremonies, the fanahy becomes a benevolent razana (ancestor spirit). If neglected, it may become an angatra (malevolent ghost) that haunts graves and brings misfortune. The fanahy represents the ongoing moral presence of the dead within the community of the living
source: Malagasy folk religion — Fanahy spirit documented in Malagasy belief.

name: Farsakh
description: The Farsakh is a legendary giant from Tajik folklore and oral tradition of the Pamir Mountains region. These immense beings are credited with constructing the ancient fortresses, terraced irrigation systems, and stone bridges that still dot the mountainous Tajik landscape. The name Farsakh connects to Persianate mythology where giants (divs or ghuls) were both builders and destroyers. In Pamiri tradition, the Farsakh represents the primordial labor that shaped the harsh mountain environment into habitable land. Legends tell of these giants moving boulders the size of houses, carving irrigation channels that still water terraced fields today, and building defensive walls across mountain passes. The giants worked primarily at night, when their immense strength was magnified. They are sometimes associated with the legendary one-armed builder Hasan, who constructed fortresses across Khorasan and the Pamirs after losing his right arm
source: Tajik Persian folklore — Farsakh giant figure.

name: Fenrir
description: Monstrous wolf - son of Loki + giantess Angrboða. Siblings: Jörmungandr (Midgard Serpent) + Hel (underworld). Old Norse: 'Fen-dweller' or 'Fenrisúlfr.' Prophecy foretold he would destroy gods. The gods tried Three fetters: (1) Laeding (broke), (2) Dromi (broke), (3) Gleipnir - made by dwarves from Impossible things: sound of cat's footsteps, woman's beard, mountain roots, fish's breath, bird's spit, bear's nerves. Looks like silk ribbon but unbreakable. The gods Tricked him - said 'test your strength.' Fenrir knew if he couldn't break it, they'd never free him. He agreed Only if Tyr put his hand in his mouth as pledge. When Fenrir couldn't break Gleipnir, Tyr lost his hand. Fenrir BIT OFF TYR'S Hand. Now bound to rock Gleipnir until Ragnarök. A sword is stuck in his jaw to gag him. At Ragnarök: Breaks Free, Swallows Odin. Odin's son Vidar kills him by stabbing heart or tearing jaws apart
source: Norse mythology, Poetic Edda & Prose Edda

name: Fetch
description: The Fetch is a spectral double or apparition of a living person in Irish and Northern English folklore, regarded as an omen of impending death. The term likely derives from Hiberno-English adaptation of Old Irish faith meaning seer, or from Old English faecce found in medieval glossaries. In 19th-century collections by John and Michael Banim, the fetch appears as an exact duplicate whose sighting carries profound significance. If seen in the evening, the fetch portends imminent death; snip snip if seen in the morning it may signal a long life ahead. The concept shares similarities with the Germanic doppelganger, the Norse fylgja, and the Scottish wraith. Francis Grose associated the term with Northern England in his 1787 Provincial Glossary. Patrick Kennedy's 1866 Legendary Fiction of the Irish Celts includes The Doctor's Fetch, where a physician's double appears to his wife the night before his sudden death
source: Celtic mythology, Irish Mythological Cycle & Mabinogion

name: Finnur hin Fróði
description: Finnur hin Fróði (Finn the Wise) is the most renowned figure in Faroese wizard folklore, a legendary wise man and magic-worker associated with the 'Black Book' (Cyprianus/Svarteboken) tradition that spread across Scandinavia. In Faroese folk belief, wizards and cunning folk possessed books of black magic that could only be passed on to a willing successor. These practitioners could control weather, heal the sick, find lost objects, ward off trolls and hidden people, and counter malevolent magic. The island of Svínoy and the village of Sumba are particularly associated with wizard lore. The tradition blends pre-Norse pagan elements with later Christian mysticism — wizards were known as 'readers' (lesarar) who could read from the Black Book to achieve supernatural results. Finnur hin Fróði is celebrated in Faroese kvæði (ballads), notably in 'Finnur hin Fríði' (CCF 26), preserved in multiple transcriptions by Svabo, Hammershaimb, and others
source: Faroese folk belief and ethnographic records of island traditions.

name: Fire Keeper
description: The Fire Keeper is a sacred guardian spirit from the Charrua people of present-day Uruguay, an invisible presence that watches over and protects every fire that burns in Charrua camps. The Charrua were a semi-nomadic indigenous people of the Southern Cone who inhabited the grasslands and pampas of Uruguay and adjacent areas of Argentina and Brazil. Fire held profound spiritual significance in their animistic worldview, and the Fire Keeper embodied the sacred essence of flame itself. This spirit asked for little beyond respect, mindfulness, and gratitude from those who benefited from fire's gifts. The elders taught the young to gather wood thoughtfully, thanking the trees for their sacrifice, to kindle flames with patience while speaking words of gratitude as the first sparks caught and grew, and to never start fires carelessly or extinguish them thoughtlessly
source: Uruguayan folklore — the fire keeper nature spirit.

name: Firebird
description: Legendary Slavic magical bird - Zhar-Ptitsa (Russian: жар-птица, 'fire-bird'). PAN-Slavic: Ukrainian 'zhar-ptytsia,' Czech 'Pták Ohnivák,' Polish 'Żar-ptak,' Slovenian 'Rajska/zlata-ptica.' Etymology: 'zhar' = fire/glow. Feathers Shine Continuously even when plucked - like embers, like the sun. Symbol of Hope and unattainable beauty. Associated with golden apples granting Eternal Youth. In tales: tries to steal apples from royal orchards before dawn. Prophetic - feather can predict the future. Capturing triggers the quest. In 'Ivan Tsarevich and the Gray Wolf': quest to capture Firebird's tail feather. In 'Maryushka': gentle orphan girl receives magic. Connected to Adam/Eve: only creature who didn't taste Forbidden Fruit, rewarded with immortality through death and rebirth (like Phoenix). Symbolizes: transformation, renewal, the danger of greed
source: Slavic mythology; the Zhar-Ptitsa is a magical bird of light and fire in Russian tales.

name: Fisaga
description: Fisaga is a gentle wind spirit from Samoan mythology, personifying the light and pleasant breeze associated with fine weather. In the Samoan language, fisaga refers specifically to a gentle, pleasant wind that brings good conditions. The most famous legend involving Fisaga comes from the tale of Ti'iti'i who imprisoned the winds one by one in his canoe or calabash to control their power over the land. Ti'iti'i captured all the fierce and destructive winds, leaving only Fisaga free to roam the islands. This myth explains why the gentlest breeze remains at liberty while stronger winds must be summoned when needed. In some versions the demigod Maui is credited with the capture of the winds rather than Ti'iti'i. Fisaga represents the benevolent aspect of nature, a force that brings comfort rather than destruction. Samoan navigators traditionally called upon Fisaga for safe passage through chants and offerings
source: Samoan mythology — Fisaga is the god of the wind, documented in Samoan oral tradition.

name: Fjøsnisse
description: Fjøsnisse (barn nisse) is a specialized type of Norwegian nisse that lives specifically in the cowshed (fjøs) and cares for the cattle. While the general nisse protects the entire farm, the fjøsnisse is devoted exclusively to the welfare of the cows, goats, and other barn animals. In Norwegian folk tradition, a well-kept barn with healthy, productive cows was a sign that the fjøsnisse was content. The fjøsnisse was known to braid the tails and manes of cattle, keep the barn clean, and help during calving. If offended, he would spoil the milk, tangle the cows' tails into impossible knots, or cause the animals to fall ill. The fjøsnisse expected offerings of the first milk from a new cow or extra portions of Christmas porridge. This specialized barn spirit reflects the central importance of dairy farming in traditional Norwegian agriculture
source: Scandinavian folklore; nisse/tomte are household spirits documented in Nordic folk belief collections.

name: Fjeldvīg
description: Fjeldvig is a Danish mountain giant, known as a bjergmand or hill man, from Danish folklore inhabiting ancient burial mounds and hills across the Danish countryside. These beings belong to the broader category of bjergfolk (mountain folk), small troll-like creatures who live in a parallel world beneath the hills and mounds. Unlike fearsome giants of other traditions, Danish bjergfolk are relatively small, with the largest reaching barely a meter in height while some ride horses no bigger than cats. They dress in old-fashioned peasant clothing from the 1800s with characteristic red pointed caps. Despite their modest stature, they possess tremendous strength and are renowned as master smiths. They consider the landscape around their hills to be their property, and humans living nearby must observe certain rules of respect. The bjergfolk can become invisible at will using their magical caps
source: Danish folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Fjellvette
description: Fjellvette (mountain wight) is a nature spirit specific to the mountains of Vestlandet. The fjellvette is a type of vette (nature spirit) that guards specific peaks, mountain passes, high pastures, and rocky crags. Each mountain in Vestlandet had its own fjellvette who protected the wildlife and punished humans who showed disrespect — killing too many reindeer, scarring the mountain with mining, or building without permission. The fjellvette could create rockfalls, avalanches, and sudden storms to drive people away. However, it could also guide lost travelers to safety, reveal hidden routes over mountain passes, and grant good hunting to respectful hunters. Offerings of food or coins were left at mountain cairns to appease the fjellvette. The tradition was strongest in the high mountain areas of Jotunheimen, Hardangervidda, and the Jostedalsbreen glacier region. The fjellvette is distinct from the bergfolk (mountain people) who live inside mountains — the fjellvette is the spirit of the mountain itself, not a resident
source: Scandinavian folklore; Vættir are nature spirits of the land and water.

name: Floghamen
description: Floghamen (the flying shape) is a shape-shifting spirit from Setesdal folklore in Sørlandet. The floghamen is the spirit-form of a witch or sorcerer that flies through the air while the person's body sleeps. The term comes from flog (flight/flying) and ham (shape/form). In Setesdal tradition, certain people could send their ham (soul-form) out of their body to travel as a bird, a ball of light, or a flying shadow. The floghamen would travel vast distances — to other farms, across the mountains, or to gatherings of other floghamen. If the sleeping body was disturbed or turned around, the floghamen could not return and the person would die or go mad. The floghamen tradition is related to the Norse concept of hamfarir (shape-traveling) and shows how pre-Christian beliefs about the soul persisted in Setesdal well into the 19th century. Johannes Skar documented multiple floghamen accounts in Gamalt or Setesdal
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Forest Person
description: The Forest Person, known in Tlingit as Kooshdaa kaa or Kushtaka (land otter man), is a shape-shifting spirit from Pacific Northwest indigenous mythology, particularly among the Tlingit people whose territory extends from southeastern Alaska into Canada. These powerful supernatural beings straddle the boundary between human and animal, living where forest meets shore. According to Tlingit creation stories, the Great Raven granted the Land Otter the gift of duality, illusion, and disguise, charging them with preserving the souls of those who drowned, as drowning was considered the most horrible death preventing reincarnation. The Kushtaka serve as both rescuers and predators, saving souls from eternal dissolution while transforming them into boundary-world beings. Similar spirits appear among the Tsimshian as Watsa and the Dena'ina as Nat'ina in South Central Alaska. They are particularly associated with Thomas Bay in Alaska In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Indigenous Canadian folklore — forest person spirit documented in First Nations oral tradition.

name: Fosen-Sjøtrollet
description: Fosen-Sjøtrollet (the Fosen Sea Troll) is a sea troll said to inhabit the waters off the Fosen peninsula in Trøndelag. Unlike the mountain trolls of inland Norway, this sjøtroll (sea troll) lives in the ocean and comes ashore only at night to raid farms. The Fosen-Sjøtrollet is described as a massive, ugly creature that lives in a cave on a remote Fosen skerry, emerging at low tide to hunt for fish and seals. It has the characteristic troll aversion to sunlight — if caught above water at sunrise, it turns to stone. The many small skerries and islands along the Fosen coast are said to be sjøtroll that were caught by daylight. Unlike mountain trolls who throw boulders, the Fosen-Sjøtrollet is associated with creating dangerous tidal currents and whirlpools. Local fishermen traditionally poured iron nails into the sea before passing certain skerries to ward off the sjøtroll
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Aztec
description: The Fox Ancestor-Spirit in Aztec tradition represents cunning, intelligence, and the sacred connection between the human and divine realms. In Aztec mythology, the fox served as a messenger between gods and humanity, created by the gods from the earth itself and imbued with the ability to navigate both physical and spiritual worlds. The fox is associated with Tezcatlipoca, the god of wisdom and change, and with Huehuecoyotl, the trickster god of music dance and mischief who appears with coyote-like features. Aztec creation myths depict the fox as a mediator who helped establish harmony among all beings after the world was formed. The fox's cunning nature made it a powerful symbol in rituals where offerings were made to invoke cleverness and strategic thinking. The fourth trecena of the Aztec calendar, Xochitl meaning Flower, was associated with fox energy and trickster wisdom
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Lakota
description: In Lakota Sioux tradition, the fox known as sungila is a significant medicine animal and spirit guide associated with wisdom, cunning, and protection. The Lakota people of the Great Plains regard the fox as a powerful teacher who reveals locations of medicinal herbs to medicine men and shares expertise on escaping enemies swiftly. The Kit Fox Society (sungila okolakic'iye) was an important warrior society responsible for policing the home camp, maintaining order, and hunting for food. While the Wolf Society fought battles far from home, the Kit Fox Society protected the immediate community. The fox appears in Lakota storytelling as a trickster embodying both wisdom and folly, teaching life lessons through clever and sometimes foolish behavior. The fox spirit teaches how to travel through dangerous territory and understand courage under fire, making it a powerful ally for warriors and hunters
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Passamaquoddy
description: In Passamaquoddy tradition from Maine and the Maritime provinces of Canada, the fox is a respected animal spirit associated with cleverness, adaptability, and survival in the northern woodlands. The Passamaquoddy, part of the Wabanaki Confederacy along with the Maliseet, Mikmaq, Penobscot, and Abenaki nations, tell stories of the fox as a cunning figure outwitting larger animals through intelligence. In Wabanaki folklore, the fox appears as a trickster, sometimes helpful and sometimes mischievous, teaching lessons about respect for nature and the consequences of greed. The fox is seen as a woodland guardian possessing intimate knowledge of the forest and its creatures. Its ability to thrive at the edge of human settlements while remaining wild and elusive made it a symbol of the boundary between civilized and natural worlds. Fox tracks were considered protective symbols in Passamaquoddy tradition
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Ashanti
description: In Ashanti (Asante) tradition from present-day Ghana in West Africa, the fox is recognized as a clever and resourceful animal spirit with a significant place in folklore and spiritual beliefs. The Ashanti people have a rich tradition of animal stories known as anansesem (spider stories) where animals illustrate moral lessons about human behavior. While Anansi the Spider is the primary trickster, the fox appears as a cunning creature using intelligence to survive in challenging situations. The fox is associated with the forest and the boundary between human settlements and the wild. Ashanti hunters regarded the fox with respect, seeing its tracks as indicators of forest health and the presence of game. The fox's elusiveness and nocturnal habits made it a symbol of strategic thinking, patience, and the ability to move unseen through dangerous territory
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of West Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of the Akan, Yoruba, Dogon, and Igbo cultures.

name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Baloch
description: In Baloch tradition from the Balochistan region spanning Iran, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, the fox is valued for its cunning and survival skills in the harsh desert environment. Baloch folklore includes numerous stories featuring the fox as a trickster using wit and deception to overcome challenges, reflecting life in arid lands where intelligence matters more than strength. The fox is associated with rocky hills, dry riverbeds, and sparse vegetation of Balochistan, surviving through adaptability and keen awareness. In Baloch proverbs and folk tales, the fox exemplifies cleverness in adversity, teaching lessons about patience, observation, and strategic thinking. The Baloch people, traditionally nomadic herders and farmers, observed fox behavior for signs about water sources and environmental conditions in their difficult landscape. The fox's ability to thrive where resources are scarce makes it a powerful symbol of resilience
source: Regional survey of South Asian folklore and mythology — Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and indigenous traditions of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bhutan as documented in sacred texts and regional folklore collections.

name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Kikuyu
description: In Kikuyu (Gikuyu) tradition from Kenya in East Africa, the fox appears in oral literature as a clever and adaptable animal spirit associated with wisdom and survival. The Kikuyu people have a rich storytelling tradition featuring animal characters that embody human virtues and vices, teaching moral lessons around the fireside. The fox appears as a creature of intelligence and resourcefulness, finding creative solutions through wit rather than physical strength. In Kikuyu cosmology as established by Ngai the Supreme God, each animal carries specific meanings and teachings for humanity. The fox's ability to thrive in diverse environments from savanna to forest edges demonstrates versatility and adaptability as core virtues. Fox behavior is observed for practical knowledge about the landscape, and encounters with foxes are interpreted as signs or omens conveying messages from the spirit world about health, weather, and fortune
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of East Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Madagascar.
